title: CSV, JSON, Parquet
story:
Three formats, three different answers to the question of what a row is, and each answer costs something specific.

Start with the one everybody assumes is settled. There is an RFC for comma separated values, and reading it is instructive, because it spends its opening paragraph admitting it has no authority. RFC 4180 is filed as Informational, it says of itself that it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and its introduction notes that, surprisingly, while this format is very common, it has never been formally documented. Its interoperability section is blunter still: due to lack of a single specification, there are considerable differences among implementations. Every parser you have ever used is guessing, in its own dialect, and the dialects disagree about the parts that matter — quoting, escaping, and what a line break means. The document does specify that a double quote inside a field is escaped by doubling it, and that a field may contain a line break provided it is quoted, which is how a single cell of free text can legally contain the record separator and split one row into two.

The tree format has the opposite problem: a real standard, and a hole in the middle of it. RFC 8259 is on the standards track, and it declines to fix number precision. It allows implementations to set limits on the range and precision of numbers accepted, and observes that since double precision arithmetic is widely available, good interoperability can be achieved by implementations that expect no more precision than that. Read that as the warning it is. The document then draws the line explicitly: integers between minus two to the fifty-third plus one and two to the fifty-third minus one are interoperable, meaning implementations will agree on them. Two to the fifty-third is 9007199254740992. A 64-bit database identifier is larger than that, and it does not survive the trip. The same document says object names SHOULD be unique, and that when they are not, the behaviour of software receiving the object is unpredictable — some parsers keep the last pair, some error, some return every duplicate.

The third format changes the axis. Parquet began in 2013 as a joint effort between engineers at Twitter and Cloudera and became a top level Apache Software Foundation project in 2015, and it stores columns rather than rows. The consequence is the reason it exists: reading three fields out of three hundred costs three columns, not three hundred, because the other two hundred and ninety-seven are never touched. Nested structures are handled by the record shredding and assembly algorithm from the Dremel paper, published by Melnik and colleagues at VLDB in 2010 — definition and repetition levels, rather than flattening the nesting away. What you give up is legibility: it is a binary file with a schema inside it, and you cannot open it in an editor and see what went wrong.

Which is the real trade. Text you can read and cannot trust; binary you can trust and cannot read.

problem.name: Serialisation format
problem.shape: Data has to leave memory and come back, and what survives the trip is decided by the format rather than by the data.
tell: types are re-inferred on every read, and sometimes differently
identifiers are large integers and they cross a process boundary
a query reads a handful of fields out of a very wide table
a free-text column contains quotes, commas or newlines that came from a human
problem.move: Choose the format from what has to survive. If types and precision matter, use a format that carries a schema. If identifiers cross a boundary, send them as strings. If the reads are narrow and the tables wide, store columns rather than rows. And whichever you pick, assert the schema on the way in rather than trusting the parser's inference.
problem.invariant: A format guarantees only what its specification guarantees, and no parser can restore information the format did not carry. Type, precision and missingness either survive the encoding or they are gone.
problem.breaks: The guarantee is about the format, not about the two implementations either side of it. Two conforming parsers can still disagree wherever the specification left a choice open — escaping, duplicate keys, number precision, the meaning of an empty field — so conformance on both ends is not the same as agreement between them.

cost.time: schema assertion on read, and for columnar formats an encoding step on write that is more expensive than appending a line of text
cost.space: columnar files compress far better because a column is homogeneous; text rows are larger and need every value re-parsed on every read
cost.beats: inferring types on read and hoping, which works until the day a column of identifiers arrives with a letter in it, or an empty field changes an integer column into a float one

worked.problem: After a round trip through one of these formats, the last digits of your identifiers have changed and a join has started dropping rows. Why, and why did nothing raise?
worked.reasoning:
Because the format you passed them through does not promise to keep them.

RFC 8259 is explicit about where the promise stops. Integers between minus two to the fifty-third plus one and two to the fifty-third minus one are interoperable — implementations will agree exactly on their values. Outside that window there is no such guarantee, because the specification allows implementations to set their own limits on range and precision, and the practical limit nearly everywhere is double precision floating point.

Two to the fifty-third is 9007199254740992. Above it, the gap between representable values is 2, so consecutive integers can no longer each have their own representation: two adjacent identifiers land on the same value, and the difference between them is gone. A 64-bit identifier — the default primary key in most databases — is routinely larger than that window, and identifiers are exactly the kind of number where being close is worthless.

Nothing errors, and that is the design. The parser is behaving correctly by its own specification; it never claimed precision it was not given. The symptom is that the last few digits of large identifiers change, a join silently drops rows that should have matched, or two distinct records merge into one.

The remedy is to stop treating an identifier as a number. Serialise it as a string, since it was never arithmetic in the first place — nobody adds two identifiers together. If you cannot change the producer, parse with a reader that supports arbitrary precision integers and be certain it is applied before the value reaches a double.

The wider lesson generalises past this format. Whenever data crosses a boundary, ask what the receiving side guarantees rather than what the sending side intended — and read the interoperability section, which is where specifications write down what they could not make everyone agree on.
worked.code:
WHAT A ROW IS, THREE WAYS

  CSV      a line of text
             no governing spec. RFC 4180 is
             Informational and says so.
             "considerable differences among
              implementations"

             a quoted field may contain the
             record separator:

                id,note
                1,"line one
                line two"          <- ONE row

             types: none. everything is text.
             you re-guess them on every read.

  JSON     a tree
             standards track, but precision is
             left to the implementation.

             safe integers:
                [-(2^53)+1, (2^53)-1]
                2^53 = 9007199254740992

             above that, spacing is 2:
                9007199254740992  ->  ...992
                9007199254740993  ->  ...992   COLLIDE

             a 64-bit id does not fit.
             -> serialise ids as STRINGS.

             duplicate keys: "SHOULD be unique";
             otherwise "unpredictable".

  PARQUET  a set of columns
             binary, schema inside the file.
             read 3 of 300 fields -> pay for 3.
             nesting via Dremel shredding
             (definition + repetition levels).

             cost: unreadable in an editor.

THE TRADE, IN ONE LINE

  text you can read and cannot trust
  binary you can trust and cannot read

problem.practice: Write a table with a 64-bit identifier, a float, an empty field and a free-text column containing a comma, a double quote and a newline. Save it to each of the three formats and read it back. Compare every value against the original — not the shape, the values — and write down which format lost what.

beats.broke: Data has to be written down somewhere, and the format decides what survives the round trip: the types, the precision, the record boundaries, and how many columns you must read in order to read one.
beats.fix: Three answers to what a row is. Comma separated text, with no governing authority — its own RFC is Informational and says it does not specify a standard of any kind. A standards track tree, which declines to fix number precision. And a binary columnar layout with a schema, using the shredding algorithm from the Dremel paper for nesting.
beats.cost: Text rows lose every type and their parsers disagree about escaping. The tree silently rounds anything past two to the fifty-third, which is where 64-bit identifiers live. The columnar file is trustworthy and cannot be opened in an editor when something goes wrong.

interview.q: After a round trip through one of these formats, the last digits of your identifiers have changed and a join has started dropping rows. Why, and why did nothing raise?
interview.trap: Blaming the parser, or reaching for a bigger numeric type on the receiving side. The parser is conforming; the guarantee simply stops at two to the fifty-third, and no type on the reading end can recover digits the encoding already discarded.
interview.answer:
Because the format does not promise to preserve them, and it says so.

The specification guarantees interoperability only for integers between minus two to the fifty-third plus one and two to the fifty-third minus one. Outside that window implementations are permitted to set their own limits on range and precision, and in practice that limit is double precision floating point.

Two to the fifty-third is 9007199254740992, and above it the spacing between representable values is 2 — so consecutive integers stop having distinct representations and two adjacent identifiers collapse onto the same value. A 64-bit primary key is comfortably outside the safe window, and an identifier is precisely the kind of number for which nearly right is worthless.

Nothing raises, because nothing is broken. The parser is meeting its own specification, which never promised more. What you see instead is the tail digits of large identifiers changing, a join quietly dropping rows that should have matched, or two records merging into one.

The fix is to stop sending identifiers as numbers. They are labels, not quantities — nobody sums two identifiers — so serialise them as strings. If the producer cannot be changed, parse with a reader that keeps arbitrary precision integers, and make sure that happens before the value is ever put into a double, because by then the information is gone.

The general habit is to ask what the receiving side guarantees rather than what the sending side intended, and to read the interoperability section of any specification, which is where the authors record what they could not make everyone agree on.

blueprint:
THREE FORMATS, THREE LOSSES

   CSV      loses TYPES
              and has no authority to appeal to.
              RFC 4180: "does not specify an
              Internet standard of any kind"

   JSON     loses PRECISION past 2^53
              2^53 = 9007199254740992
              above it the gap is 2, so
              adjacent ids collide.
              -> ids are strings, not numbers.

   PARQUET  loses LEGIBILITY
              binary + schema. columnar, so
              3 of 300 fields costs 3.
              nesting: Dremel shredding, 2010.

THE QUESTION TO ASK AT ANY BOUNDARY

   not "what did the sender mean"
   but "what does the RECEIVER guarantee"

   and then read the interoperability section,
   which is where a spec writes down what it
   could not make everyone agree on.

THE TELL THAT YOU HAVE BEEN BITTEN

   the last digits of large ids changed
   a join silently dropped rows
   two distinct records became one

   none of it raised. nothing was broken.
   the parser met its own spec.
takeaway: A format guarantees only what its specification guarantees — comma separated text has no authority at all, the tree format stops promising integers past two to the fifty-third where 64-bit identifiers live, and the columnar file trades legibility for a schema and for reading three fields out of three hundred.
